typical: a plane/ship goes down. NOT for: prices falling.
The plane went down shortly after midnight.
The ship went down in the storm.
go for: verb
attack or criticize someone
typical: go for sb. NOT for: defending.
The dog went for me.
The newspapers went for her.
verb
try to get or win something
typical: go for gold/a prize/it. NOT for: giving up.
Jackson is going for his second gold medal.
If you want the job, go for it!
verb
choose something
typical: go for the chocolate cake. NOT for: refusing.
I think I'll go for the chocolate cake.
They went for the cheaper option.
verb
would like to have or do something (spoken)
typical: I could go for sth. NOT for: refusing.
A full meal for under five euros? I could go for that!
I could go for a coffee right now.
go in for: take an examination or enter a competition (BrE)
typical: go in for an exam/a contest. NOT for: skipping.
I'd like to go in for competitions.
He went in for the race.
do or use something often because you like it
typical: go in for sports/gardening. NOT for: avoiding.
I never really went in for sports.
She doesn't go in for jewellery.
typical: go in for law/teaching. NOT for: leaving.
I could go in for advertising.
go into: verb
start working in a type of job or profession
typical: go into nursing/business/politics. NOT for: leaving.
I always wanted to go into nursing.
She's thinking of going into business.
verb
be spent on something (time, money or effort)
typical: a lot of work/money goes into sth. NOT for: wasting.
Years of research went into this book.
A lot of time has gone into it.
verb
describe or study something in detail
typical: go into detail/the facts. NOT for: skipping.
I can't go into details now.
He went into the matter.
verb
enter a place or a state
typical: go into a room/shock/debt. NOT for: leaving.
She went into the room.
He went into shock.
go off: verb
explode, used about a bomb
typical: a bomb goes off. NOT for: exploding by hand.
The bomb went off in the empty station.
A bomb went off near the market.
verb
make a loud noise, used about an alarm or a gun
typical: an alarm/gun goes off. NOT for: switching off.
The alarm went off at three a.m.
A gun went off nearby.
verb
become too old to eat, used about food (BrE)
typical: milk/food goes off. NOT for: fresh food.
The milk has gone off.
The fish went off in the heat.
verb
stop working, used about power or lights
typical: the lights/heating go off. NOT for: starting up.
The lights suddenly went off.
The heating goes off at ten.
go on: verb
continue doing something, or continue without stopping
typical: go on doing sth, go on with sth, go on and on. NOT for: happening or doing something next.
She went on working until midnight.
The noise went on all night.
verb
happen
typical: what's going on?, there's a lot going on. NOT for: continuing.
What's going on in there?
There is a lot going on this week.
verb
do something after you have finished something else
typical: go on to do sth, go on to the next + noun. NOT for: continuing the same activity.
He went on to become a doctor.
Let's go on to the next question.
verb
used to encourage someone to do something (spoken)
typical: Go on!, Go on, try it. NOT for: describing continuing.
Go on, have another piece of cake.
Go on, you can do it!
go out: verb
leave your home to enjoy yourself
typical: go out for a meal/for a drink, go out tonight. NOT for: romantic relationships.
Are you going out tonight?
We went out for dinner.
verb
have a romantic relationship with someone
typical: go out with sb, go out together. NOT for: leaving the house for fun.
They have been going out for two years.
She used to go out with my brother.
verb
stop burning or shining
typical: a light/fire/candle goes out. NOT for: being broadcast.
The candle suddenly went out.
The fire went out in the night.
verb
stop playing in a competition because you lost
typical: go out in the first round. NOT for: leaving the house.
He went out in the first round.
The team went out of the cup.
go over: verb
check or examine something carefully
typical: go over sth (a report/accounts/plan). NOT for: visiting.
The teacher went over my essay.
Go over your work before you hand it in.
verb
explain or repeat something to make sure it is clear
typical: go over the main points/the rules. NOT for: checking quietly.
Let's go over the instructions once more.
The coach went over the game plan.
verb
be received in a particular way
typical: go over well/badly. NOT for: examining.
The joke didn't go over well.
The new policy went over badly with staff.
verb
visit someone, usually nearby
typical: go over to sb's house. NOT for: checking carefully.
I'm going over to Anna's tonight.
We went over to the neighbours for coffee.
go round: verb
move in a circle
typical: go round and round, the wheel goes round. NOT for: moving straight.
The wheels went round faster and faster.
My head is going round.
verb
visit someone's home
typical: go round to sb's house. NOT for: going far away.
I'll go round to Anna's after dinner.
Why don't you go round and see him?
verb
be enough for everyone
typical: there is enough to go round. NOT for: not enough.
There isn't enough pizza to go round.
Will the food go round?
verb
travel around a place or building
typical: go round a museum, go round the corner. NOT for: visiting a friend.
We went round the castle in an hour.
The bus goes round the whole town.
go through: verb
experience something difficult or unpleasant
typical: go through a crisis/divorce/hard time. NOT for: easy things.
She went through a difficult time.
He is going through a divorce.
verb
experience a process or series of stages
typical: go through stages/a process. NOT for: skipping steps.
Candidates go through a selection process.
Caterpillars go through several stages.
verb
be officially accepted, used about a law or deal
typical: a law/deal/sale goes through. NOT for: falling through.
The deal went through.
The new law went through Parliament.
verb
practise or repeat something from start to finish
typical: go through a performance/a speech. NOT for: starting.
Let's go through the whole thing again.
She went through her speech twice.
go through with: do something you promised or planned, even though it is hard
typical: go through with sth, go through with it. NOT for: giving up.
He went through with the wedding.
I had no choice but to go through with it.
go together: typical: two things go together. NOT for: being separate.
Alcohol abuse and eating disorders often go together.
look good or taste good together
typical: colours/foods go together. NOT for: clashing.
Red and green don't go together.
go under: stop operating because of money problems (a business)
typical: a business goes under. NOT for: opening.
More than 7,000 businesses have gone under.
sink below the surface of water
typical: go under (the water). NOT for: floating.
go up: verb
increase in price, amount or level
typical: prices/costs/temperatures go up, go up by 10%. NOT for: becoming smaller.
Train fares have gone up again.
Unemployment went up by a million.
verb
be built or fixed in place
typical: buildings/signs/tents go up. NOT for: being destroyed.
New houses are going up everywhere.
A huge sign went up over the entrance.
verb
explode or be destroyed by fire
typical: the building/car went up in flames. NOT for: prices rising.
The whole kitchen went up in flames.
The car hit the wall and went up.
verb
if a shout or cheer goes up, people suddenly begin to shout or cheer
typical: a cheer/cry/shout goes up. NOT for: a price increase.
A great cheer went up from the crowd.
A cry went up when the goal was scored.
go with: verb
be included as part of something
typical: a house goes with a job. NOT for: separate things.
A car goes with the job.
The garden goes with the flat.
verb
look good or be suitable with something else
typical: go with a colour/a dress/a meal. NOT for: clashing.
Red wine goes well with beef.
That tie doesn't go with your shirt.
verb
accept or choose a plan or idea
typical: go with the idea/plan/flow. NOT for: rejecting.
Let's go with your idea.
We decided to go with the cheaper option.
verb
often exist together with something else, or be related to it
typical: sth goes with sth. NOT for: being unrelated.
Ill health often goes with poverty.
Responsibility goes with the job.
go without: not have something you usually have
typical: go without (sth). NOT for: having enough.
I'd rather go without than borrow.
it goes without saying: used when something is obvious
typical: it goes without saying (that). NOT for: new facts.
It goes without saying that the Internet is a good source.
It goes without saying that you must be on time.
granted: admits that something is true before you make your main point
typical: at the start of a sentence, spoken or written. NOT for: the verb meaning 'give permission'.
Granted, the price is high, but the quality is excellent.
Granted, he made a mistake. Still, he apologised.
It is expensive, granted, but it will last.
grow apart: become less close in a relationship over time
typical: grow apart over the years. NOT for: growing closer.
The couple had been growing apart for years.
grow into: develop over time into a particular type of person or thing
typical: grow into a man/a woman/sth. NOT for: staying the same.
Sue grew into a lovely young woman.
The show grew into a series.
gradually learn how to do a job or deal with a situation
typical: grow into a role/job. NOT for: feeling ready at once.
She will grow into her new role.
become big enough to wear clothes (a child)
typical: grow into clothes. NOT for: growing out of them.
The coat's too big, but he'll grow into it.
She will grow into the shoes.
grow out of: become too big to wear clothes (a child)
typical: grow out of clothes/shoes. NOT for: growing into them.
He grew out of his shoes.
She has grown out of her coat.
stop doing something as you get older
typical: grow out of a habit/a phase. NOT for: starting.
Mike is growing out of his rebelliousness.
Most children grow out of it.
develop or happen as a result of something
typical: grow out of sth. NOT for: ending.
His art grew out of his love of nature.
The law grew out of public concern.
grow up: develop from a child into an adult
typical: grow up in/as/to be. NOT for: staying young.
What do you want to be when you grow up?
behave in a more responsible way (spoken)
typical: Grow up!. NOT for: acting childish.
start to exist and develop gradually
typical: a town/trade grows up. NOT for: disappearing.
Trading settlements grew up by the river.
A custom grew up around it.
